ex-E102-1.title: Period of Saturn
ex-E102-1.question:
Saturn moves along an elliptical orbit around the Sun. Its perihelion is

1.35 × 1012 m from the Sun and its aphelion is 1.51 × 1012 m from the Sun.

(a) Find the semi-major axis of Saturn.

(b) The semi-major axis of the Earth is 1 AU (= 1.50 × 1011 m). Find the

orbital period of Saturn.
ex-E102-1.answer:
(a) Semi-major axis a = 12 × (1.35 × 1012 + 1.51 × 1012) = 1.43 × 1012 m

(b) Consider Saturn and the Earth. By Kepler’s third law,

T2TEarth2 = a3aEarth3

T212 = (1.43 × 1012)3(1.50 × 1011)3

T = 29.4 years

Alternative method:

Semi-major axis a = 1.43 × 10121.50 × 1011 = 9.53 AU

By Kepler’s third law,

T2TEarth2 = a3aEarth3

T212 = 9.53313

T = 29.4 years
ex-E102-1.tips:
Tip

Express both T in years and both a in metres.

Tip

Express both T in years and both a in AU.
ex-E102-1.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 7

ex-E102-2.title: Galilean satellites
ex-E102-2.question:
The Galilean satellites are the four largest satellites of Jupiter. Io is one of them. The orbital period and semi-major axis of Io are 42.5 hours and

4.22 × 108 m respectively.

(a) The orbit of Io is nearly circular. Estimate the average orbital speed of Io.

(b) Europa is another Galilean satellite. The orbital period of Europa is 3.55 days. Find the semi-major axis of Europa.

(c) The orbital period of the Earth’s satellite, the Moon, is 27.3 days. Can we use the above data to estimate the semi-major axis of the Moon by applying Kepler’s third law? Explain your answer.
ex-E102-2.answer:
(a) For a circular orbit, a = r.

Average orbital speed = 2πrT = 2π(4.22 × 108)42.5 × 60 × 60 = 17 300 m s–1

(b) By Kepler’s third law,

T12T22 = a13a23

(3.55 × 24)242.52 = a13(4.22 × 108)3

a1 = 6.71 × 108 m

The semi-major axis of Europa is 6.71 × 108 m.

(c) No, because the Moon is orbiting the Earth, not the same celestial body that Io is orbiting.
ex-E102-2.tips:
Tip

Express both T in hours and both a in metres.
ex-E102-2.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 8

ex-E102-3.title: Comet Halley
ex-E102-3.question:
Comet Halley orbits the Sun in an elliptical path as shown below. R is the furthest position of Comet Halley from the Sun. P and Q are two positions on its orbit. Take the orbital period of the comet as 75.3 years. The shortest distance between the comet and the Sun is 0.586 AU.

(a) Find the distance x between R and the Sun.

(b) Comet Halley last appeared at the closest position from the Sun in February 1986. Estimate the year in which it returns to R for the first time after that.

(c) Where does Comet Halley have a higher speed, at P or Q? Explain briefly.
ex-E102-3.answer:
(a) Consider Comet Halley and the Earth. By Kepler’s third law,

T2TEarth2 = a3aEarth3

75.3212 = a313

a = 17.83 AU

By definition of semi-major axis,

a = 12 × (0.586 + x) = 17.83

x = 35.1 AU

(b) 12 × 75.3 = 37.65 years

The year Comet Halley first returned to R = 1986 + 37 = 2023

(c) Comet Halley has a higher speed at P as P is closer to the Sun than Q.
ex-E102-3.tips:
Tip

Express both T in years and both a in AU.

Tip

An orbiting body takes half of its orbital period to move from perihelion to aphelion.

Tip

Comet Halley is at the perihelion in February. Take this into account,

with 212 = 0.17 years,

1986.17 + 37.65 = 2023.82

∴ The answer is 2023.
ex-E102-3.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 9

ex-E102-4.title: Artificial satellites around the Earth
ex-E102-4.question:
An artificial satellite is launched to orbit the Earth at an altitude of 250 km above the Earth’s surface.

Take the mass and radius of the Earth as 5.97 × 1024 kg and 6370 km

respectively. Given: G = 6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2

(a) (i) Find the orbital speed of the satellite.

(ii) If the satellite orbits the Earth at a higher altitude, would the orbital speed be higher or lower than that in (a)? Explain briefly.

(b) (i) Find the orbital period (in hours) of the satellite.

(ii) Another artificial satellite takes twice the time to orbit the Earth once. Estimate its orbital radius.
ex-E102-4.answer:
(a) (i) As the gravitational force provides the centripetal force,

mv2r=GMmr2

v=GMr

=(6.67×10−11)(5.97×1024)(250+6370)×103=7760 m s−1

The orbital speed of the satellite is 7760 m s-1.

(ii) According to v=GMr, the orbital speed v would be lower if the orbital radius r is greater.

(b) (i) By Kepler’s third law,

T2=(4π2GM)r3

T=(4π2GM)r3

=[4π2(6.67×10−11)(5.97×1024)][(250+6370)×103]3

=5360 s=1.49 h

The orbital period of the satellite is 1.49 hours.

(ii) By T2∝ r3,

T12T22=r13r23

(2T2)2T22=r13[(250+6370)×103]3

r1=1.05×107 m

The orbital radius of the other satellite is 1.05×107 m.
ex-E102-4.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 12, 13

ex-E102-5.title: Satellites of different planets
ex-E102-5.question:
Satellite X of mass m orbits around planet A of mass M, with M >> m, in a circular orbit of radius r. Its orbital speed is v and orbital period is T.

(a) Using Newton’s law of gravitation, show that T2 = 4π2r3GM.

(b) Another satellite Y of mass 2m orbits around planet B of mass 3M in a circular orbit of radius 3r. Find its period in terms of T.
ex-E102-5.answer:
(a) As the gravitational force provides the centripetal force,

GMmr2 = mv2r

v2 = GMr

Since T = 2πrv,

T2 = 4π2r2v2 = 4π2r2(GMr) = 4π2r3GM

(b) Since T2 = 4π2r3GM, T2 ∝ r3M

TY2TX2 = rY3rX3 × MAMB

TY2T2 = (3r)3r3 × M3M

TY = 3T

Period of satellite Y is 3T. Exercise 2.1 Q10 (p.62)
ex-E102-5.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 14

ex-E102-6.title: Orbital period of Tiangong
ex-E102-6.question:
The Tiangong space station is in a low Earth elliptical orbit. The closest point and the furthest point are 389.5 km and 395 km above the Earth’s surface respectively. Take the mass and radius of the Earth to be 5.97 × 1024 kg and 6370 km respectively. Find the orbital period (in hours) of the Tiangong space station.

Given: G = 6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2
ex-E102-6.answer:
Semi-major axis a=12×[(389.5+6370)+(395+6370)]=6762 km

By Kepler’s third law for elliptical orbits,

T2=(4π2GM)a3

T=(4π2GM)a3

=[4π2(6.67×10−11)(5.97×1024)](6762×103)3

=5540 s=1.54 h

The orbital period of the Tiangong space station is 1.54 hours.
ex-E102-6.tips:
Tip

Divide the value by 3600 to convert it from s to h.
ex-E102-6.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 16

ex-E102-7.question:

(a) Find the potential energy U of the satellite when it is at 850 km above the ground.

(b) Find the change in potential energy ΔU of the satellite during the launch.

(c) Consider a general case when a satellite of mass m is launched from the Earth’s surface to a height of h above the Earth’s surface. Given that the radius of the Earth is R and the acceleration due to gravity on the Earth’s surface is g, show that the change in potential energy ΔU of the

satellite is mgh (RR + h).

ex-E102-9.title: Orbital speed of a spacecraft
ex-E102-9.question:
A spacecraft moves around the Earth in an elliptical orbit. The speed of the spacecraft is 1.00 × 104 m s−1 when it is at position P which is at 200 km above the Earth’s surface. Take the mass and radius of the Earth to be

5.97 × 1024 kg and 6370 km respectively.

Given: G = 6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2

(a) Find the speed of the spacecraft at position Q which is at 50 km above the Earth’s surface.

(b) The mass of the spacecraft is 1.2 × 105 kg. Find the total mechanical energy of the spacecraft at position P.

(c) If the spacecraft is powered to move from position P to infinity, what is the minimum energy needed by the spacecraft?
ex-E102-9.answer:
(a) K1 + U1 = K2 + U2

12 mv12 + (− GMmr1) = 12 mv22 + (− GMmr2)

12 v12 + (− GMr1) = 12 v22 + (− GMr2)

GM (1r2 − 1r1) = 12 (v22 − v12)

(6.67 × 10−11)(5.97 × 1024)[1(50 + 6370) × 103 − 1(200 + 6370) × 103]

= 12 [v22 − (1.00 × 104)2]

v2 = 1.01 × 104 m s−1

The speed of the spacecraft at position Q is 1.01 × 104 m s−1.

(b) Total mechanical energy at position P

= 12 mv12 + (− GMmr1)

= 12 × (1.2 × 105) × (1.00 × 104)2 + [− (6.67 × 10−11)(5.97 × 1024)(1.2 × 105)(200 + 6370) × 103]

= −1.27 × 1012 J

(c) The minimum total energy of the spacecraft at infinity is 0.

∴ The minimum energy needed is 1.27 × 1012 J.
ex-E102-9.think: If the spacecraft is powered to move from position Q to infinity, what is the minimum energy needed by the spacecraft?
ex-E102-9.thinkAnswer: The same amount, 1.27×1012 J. Mechanical energy is conserved along the unpowered orbit, so the total at Q equals that at P, −1.27×1012 J. The minimum total energy for escape to infinity is zero. Thus Δ E=0−(−1.27×1012)=1.27×1012 J.
ex-E102-9.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 29

ex-E102-10.title: Escape velocity from the Earth
ex-E102-10.question:
The mass and radius of the Earth are 5.97 × 1024 kg and 6370 km respectively. Find the escape velocity

(a) from the Earth’s surface,

(b) from a height of 200 km above the Earth’s surface.

Given: G = 6.67 × 10−11 N m2 kg−2
ex-E102-10.answer:
(a) Escape velocity from the Earth’s surface

= 2GMR = 2 × (6.67 × 10−11) × (5.97 × 1024)6370 × 103 = 11 200 m s−1

(b) Escape velocity from a height of 200 km above the Earth’s surface

= 2GMr = 2 × (6.67 × 10−11) × (5.97 × 1024)(200 + 6370) × 103 = 11 000 m s−1
ex-E102-10.location: Book E1  |  Chapter E102  |  Source PDF p. 32
